translations.text: Of the same our holy father Basil: a discourse on the beginning of the Gospel of John, namely: "In the beginning was the Word."
All the words of the four Gospels stand above all the other teachings of the Spirit,
for in the other books he spoke to us through his servants the prophets, but in the Gospel the King of all conversed with us in his own person.
Yet within the very preaching of the evangelists, the one above all is the loud-voiced John, who speaks beyond all hearing and higher than all understanding,
that son of thunder, the beginning of whose written Gospel we have just now read aloud and heard:
"In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."
I have seen many of those who are outside the word of truth,
who pride themselves on the wisdom of this vain world, marvel at these words and presume to set them down in their own writings.
For the devil is a thief, and he carries off what is ours to his own servants.
Now if fleshly wisdom so marveled at the power of these words, what then shall we do, we who are disciples of the Spirit?
Shall we listen carelessly and reckon the power within them as small? And who would be so seized by madness
as not to marvel at such beauty of theology and at a depth of understanding so unattainable, and not to long to attain their true power?
But it is not difficult merely to marvel at good things; what is difficult is for a person to attain, with true comprehension, the things at which he marvels.
This is hard to find. For even in the case of this visible sun, there is no one who would not praise its greatness and goodness, the beauty of its rays, and its light.
But if someone should wish to fix his eyes on it more intently, not only can he not observe it well, but even the sight he had before is darkened as well.
So it is also with the mind that strives to find a true understanding of these words set before us: "In the beginning was the Word."
Who could worthily understand this "beginning"? What power of speech could be found to declare in such a way what has been understood?
For when this great and lofty man, likened to the seraphim, was about to speak to us on the theology of the Son of God,
he did not wish to make any other beginning for his discourse than that which is first of all.
For the Holy Spirit knew those who were to come, who would fight against and blaspheme the divinity of the Only-begotten;
he knew beforehand the wickedness of those who would use much talk to subvert those who obeyed them, saying:
"If he was born, he was not; before his birth he was not, and he received his being from nothing."
For this is how those tongues speak, sharpened by blasphemy more than any two-edged sword.
But so that no one might be able to say such words, the Holy Spirit anticipated them and moved the evangelist, and through him he said:
"In the beginning was the Word." If you hold firmly to this saying, you will in no way be harmed by those evil breeds.
If that person says, "If he was born, he was not," you say, "In the beginning he was."
If he says to you again, "And before birth, how was he?" do not depart from the word "was"; do not abandon "in the beginning."
No head or origin of that Beginning is found; there is nothing prior to that Beginning.
Let the many senses of this word not lead you astray, for many things in this life are called "beginning."
But the Beginning that is supreme over all is one. For it says, "The beginning of the good way," as Solomon said.
But the beginning of a way is its starting point, from which we began to walk, and an end of it is found. And again:
"The beginning, the origin of wisdom, is the fear of the Lord." And does not something else lie before this as well?

The beginning of the arts is instruction, and the instruction of wisdom is the fear of the Lord; and prior to this is the constitution of the soul, which has not yet received wisdom and the fear of the Lord.
Those in authority and the rulers of cities are also called "beginnings," but all these beginnings are the beginnings of some matter, and they move toward something.
For letters are prior to the joining together of words.
But that Beginning is not like this: it is nailed to nothing, it is bound to nothing, it serves no one,
it is seen together with no one, but it is free, without a master, released from looking toward anything else, unreachable by the mind,
which the mind cannot surpass or keep pace with, and prior to which it is impossible to find anything.
For if you strive by the sight of the mind to keep pace with that Beginning, you will find it going before you and meeting you ahead of your thoughts.
Let such a mind go, so that it may run as far as it wishes and stretch out toward the height.
Then you will find it to have wandered countless times, greatly wearied in vain, and turned back upon itself,
when it has been unable to bring that Beginning under itself, for that Beginning is always found outside and higher than whatever has been conceived.
"In the beginning, then, was the Word." O wonder! How all these words are joined with one another in equality!
For "was" has equal force with "in the beginning." Where is the blasphemer?
Where is that tongue that fights against Christ, which says, "There was once a time when he was not"?
Hear the evangelist: "In the beginning he was." And if in the beginning he was, when was he not? What am I to do about their lawlessness?
Shall I sigh, or shall I condemn the folly of those who say, "Before birth he was not"?
And do you know when he was born, that you bring in that "before"? For "before" is a temporal word, which places one thing ahead of another in age,
but how could the Creator of times have a birth of such a kind that it could be called by a temporal term?
"In the beginning, then, he was." If you do not depart from this word "was," you will give no place at all to that evil blasphemy.
For just as a ship that is well moored on anchors on both sides has no fear of the waves, so you will rebuke this evil agitation
which has come upon the world through wicked spirits and is shaking the faith of many.
And you will treat it with contempt, if your soul is armed with the firmness of these words.
If our mind should ask who existed from the beginning, it says: "the Word." Which word? Could it be this human word, or the word of angels?
For the Apostle indicated that the angels too have their own language, when he said: "If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels."
And again, there are two kinds of "word": one is spoken with the voice and dissolves into the air after it is spoken, and the second is the one that exists within us,
which is in our hearts, the word of thought, understanding and skill. Take care that the fact that these share one name does not lead you astray.
For how could the word of a human being have existed from the beginning, when the human being was the last to receive the beginning of its existence?

For before the human being, the wild beasts and cattle were made, and all the creeping things of the waters and of the dry land, and the birds of the sky, and the sun and the moon and the stars, and the plants, and the earth and the sea and the heavens.
So the word of a human being did not exist from the beginning, and neither did the word of angels exist from the beginning,
for every created thing, having received the beginning of its existence from the Creator, is younger than the ages.
And again, the inner word of the heart is also inferior to the mind and younger than it.
But hear this word in a godly and fitting way, for he was speaking of the Only-begotten and called him "Word," just as a little later he calls him "Light" and "Life" and "Resurrection."
And when you hear "light," do not be drawn toward this visible light; and when you hear "life," do not take it to mean this ordinary life of ours, which the beasts also have.
In the same way, when you hear "Word," be careful that the weakness of your nature does not lead you toward lowly and earthly thoughts.
Instead, look into its meaning: why did he say "Word"? To show that he came forth from the mind. Why is he the Word?
Because he was begotten without passion. Why is he the Word? Because he is the image of the one who begot him and shows him completely in himself.
He is not separated from him, and he is complete in himself. For just as our word expresses the thought of our heart, and what we have conceived in the heart
we utter in speech, and the spoken word is an image of the heart's thought,
for the word comes forth out of the abundance of the heart. Our heart is like a spring, and the word is like the water that rises from that spring.
The stream is as great as what first rose up, and what is revealed is just like what is hidden.

So he said "Word" to show you the Father's begetting without passion, to speak theologically of the Son's perfect being, and to reveal through these words the timeless union of the Son with the Father.
For this word of ours is also an offspring of the mind, begotten without passion, for it is not cut off, nor divided, nor does it flow away,
Rather, the nature remains wholly and completely in its own constitution, and in this way it brings forth the complete word.
And when the word goes forth, it has in itself all the power of the mind that begot it. Now therefore, whatever is good and acceptable,
only that much take for the theology of the only-begotten Son of God from this image of our word; and whatever you find unfitting and not good to apply as an image of him,
keep away from it and pass over it by every means. "In the beginning was the Word."
But if he had said, "In the beginning was the Son," a thought of passion might perhaps have entered your mind, for among us parents beget in time and with passion.
For this reason he anticipated this and gave him the name "Word," so that he might correct those improper suspicions in advance and keep your soul unwounded.
"And the Word was with God." Again he said "was" because of those blasphemers who say, "He was not." Where was the Word?
He was not in a place, for the uncircumscribed is not confined in a place. But where was he? "With God."
Neither is the Father in a place, nor is the Son held by circumscription; rather, the Father is infinite and the Son is infinite. Everything
that you may conceive of, and wherever you may go in your spirit, you will find all of it filled by God; everywhere you will find the being of the Son joined to it.
"And the Word was with God." Marvel at the force of each word!
He did not say, "The Word was in God," but "with God," so that he might show the distinctness of the hypostasis.
He did not say "in God," so as not to give an occasion for the evil teaching of those who make a merging of the hypostases.
Evil too is the blasphemy of those who dare to confound them, who speak of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit as one hypostasis, and who contrive to apply these three names to one thing.
Evil and abominable is that lawlessness; it is worse than that of those who say that the Son of God is unlike God and the Father in nature.
These two blasphemies are equal: the merging of Sabellius and the division of Arius, the one by hypostasis and the other by nature.
"And the Word was with God." Then, when he had said this and had used this name "Word" so that the impassible begetting might be understood,
he again quickly healed the harm that was coming upon us through the name "Word."
And as if snatching himself away from the slander of the blasphemers, he said what the Word was: "And the Word was God."

Do not play the clever craftsman before me over distinctions of words, O you who are darkened in the light, and do not with that abominable conduct of yours attach any blasphemy to the teachings of the Spirit.
You have this entirely good definition; submit to the Lord, for "the Word was God." "He was in the beginning with God."
See now how with a few words he turns back again to the beginning and restates all of his theology,
which the wonderful evangelist spoke concerning the Only-begotten: "Who was the Word?" "He was God."
For since he has revealed to you the understanding of him and has inscribed in your soul by his teaching what you did not know,
And he established the word "Christ" in your heart, then turned back again and said, "This one." "This one" — who?
Do not look around outside you, seeking someone outside by this demonstrative word, but enter into the hidden places of your soul.
And just as you have been taught by this about God who was from the beginning, who came forth as a word,
who was and is with God, know this one, and marvel, and worship your King, who has entered into you through this teaching;
understand that "this one was in the beginning with God," his own Father.
These are the words spoken to us by that unlearned man, words that overthrow and burn up the tongues sharpened by vain wisdom.
But, glorious Spirit, King of the heavens, Comforter, Spirit of truth, I worship your divinity,
you who made that fisherman a proclaimer of such matters, O Trinity, my instruction and my adornment,
who granted such wisdom to that man. O man and angel, beloved of Christ, who thus taught us the truth!
O brothers, keep these few words in your souls, as though sealed with a seal.
Let these be a firm wall for you in the battle against the adversaries; these are guardians of the soul, protectors from the injury of those who do harm.
If anyone comes up to you and says to you: "He was not, and then he was born, for if he was, how was he born?"
turn away that blasphemy against the glory of the Only-Begotten as the voice of the devil, and turn back and come to these words of the Gospel:
"In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
This one was in the beginning with God." Four times he said "was," and you will do away with their "was not."
May these foundations of the faith stand unshaken. Upon them, with God's help, let us build the rest also.
For it is not possible to speak about everything at once, lest by an immoderate quantity of words we make useless for you these things gathered with labor.
For the mind becomes powerless to grasp all things equally and at once, and it is afflicted [?], like a stomach that, because of the abundance of its fullness, cannot digest what it has eaten.
But I will pray for you, that the taste may be sweet to you and the digestion profitable.
And I stand ready for the service of supplying what is lacking in what has been said, through Christ Jesus our Lord,
to whom belong glory and might, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
